text: Theo printed the rejection letter for some reason and put it in a folder with the others. There were eleven now. He filed it alphabetically. He sat at his desk. text: I had three drafts of a triumphant Instagram post saved in my notes app. They had been there for a year. The publisher said no. I deleted the drafts. text: Lena's husband sent her a YouTube link. The thumbnail was a band she didn't know, playing what was unmistakably her song. Twelve million views. text: A friend texted me a video from a wedding. "Isn't this yours?" she wrote. It was. The bride was dancing to it with her father. Both of them were crying. I watched it three times. text: Jamal read the notice twice on the bus home. The bus was crowded. A baby was crying somewhere behind him. He folded the notice and put it in his pocket. He looked out the window. text: Theresa held the notice while sitting on her son's twin bed. He was at his father's for the weekend. text: Reggie found out from a true-crime podcast his coworker had recommended. The address was familiar. The address was his. He paused the episode. He sat in his car in the work parking lot. text: I was reading the local paper's archive for a school project for my daughter when I saw the headline. The photo was my house. Same shutters. Same porch. I read the article. I read it twice. text: Anne's realtor called her, a year after the sale, voice sheepish. "There's something you should know." Anne stood in her own kitchen and listened. The story was short. text: A man came to my door asking if he could see the basement. He explained who he was. He explained what had happened. He had been a child when it happened. I listened to him for a long time. text: Eduardo came outside to find his Civic gone. He stood on the porch in his slippers, his coffee in his hand, looking at the empty patch of asphalt. He walked down the steps. text: I came back from the gym at six AM and my car wasn't there. I stood in my driveway in my sweatshirt and my breath made clouds. I checked twice that I was at the right house. I was. topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: Penelope found the maple lying across her tomato beds at dawn. The tomatoes were finished. The beds were finished. The trellises were finished. She stood in her bathrobe with her coffee. text: His pine landed on my garage. The garage I had refinished two years ago. The garage that had been my project, my pride, the place I went to think. I came home from the dentist and there it was. text: Howard's neighbor's elm had been leaning toward Howard's house for three years. He had asked, twice, gently. The neighbor had said he'd take care of it. The neighbor had not taken care of it. text: I texted my neighbor a picture of his sweetgum on my driveway. He texted back: I'll send my guy. That was four days ago. The tree is still there. text: I found out from his obituary. He had died, my neighbor of fifteen years, the man I had complained to about the bin schedule, the man who had given me tomatoes. text: Sasha sat in the dean's office, the printout in front of her, the highlighted lines accusing her of something she had not done. The dean talked. Sasha nodded. The room was warm. text: Lila's professor pulled her aside after lecture. "Walk with me?" he said. They walked across the quad. He said the paper had similarities to a paper from a previous student. He had reported it. text: Kenji opened the email on his phone in the bathroom. A 62. The professor had attached a rubric. Kenji scrolled the rubric. He flushed. He washed his hands. He looked at himself in the mirror. text: Mr. Davis handed back the tests in alphabetical order. I watched everyone get theirs. When mine came, the red number was at the top. 71. I had thought it was the easiest test of the year. I said I didn't know. I really didn't. I did my homework. I did the dishes. I did not feel like crying. I felt like sleeping for ten years.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: Renee saw the grade pop up while she was on her bike at the gym. The screen of the cardio machine read 47%. She kept pedaling. The number stayed there for the next eight minutes of her ride. She did not stop. She finished the ride. She wiped down the machine. She walked to the locker room. She showered. She sat on the bench in the locker room with her towel around her, looking at her shoes. She would email the TA. She would. She had been trying so hard. She got dressed. She went to dinner. She did not eat much.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: I had told my friends, confidently, that I had nailed it. The grade was a D. I read it walking out of the lecture hall. I kept walking. I walked all the way back to my apartment, two miles. The wind was sharp. My hands were cold. I did not put them in my pockets. I felt them get number. At my apartment, I put my key in the door. I went inside. I sat on my futon. I did not take my coat off. The cold of my hands moved up my arms, slowly. After a while I took off the coat. I made tea.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Marcus opened the results on his lunch break. He had ordered the kit as a joke for his thirty-fifth birthday. The ethnicity estimate did not match either of his parents. Not even a little. He read it twice. He closed his laptop. He ate the rest of his sandwich. He went back to work. He did not call his parents. He did not call his sister. He typed an email to a client. He attended a meeting. He drove home. He sat in the driveway for fifteen minutes. His wife came out and tapped on the window. He rolled it down. "Long day?" she said. He said yes.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: I learned at thirty-seven that my dad wasn't my dad biologically. The DNA site told me. I sat with that for a week before I told anyone. I went to work. I came home. I made dinner. I watched TV with my husband. I went to bed. I did the same things I had always done. The information sat next to me in the passenger seat. It did not say anything. It just sat there. I would talk to my mom. I would. After Thanksgiving. After Christmas. After the new year. I felt like I had aged ten years in seven days, and not loudly. Quietly. The way old wood ages.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Ramona's results showed a half-sister she had never heard of, with eighty percent shared DNA with her father. She closed the website. She made dinner. She fed her kids. She helped them with homework. She gave them their baths. She read them their stories. She put them to bed. She sat on the couch. She looked at the wall. The DVR menu had been on the same screen for an hour. She did not pick up the remote. Her husband came in and sat next to her. He did not ask. She did not tell. She would. Eventually. Her eyes were heavy. She did not move.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: I cried for ten minutes when I read the results. Then I stopped. Then I felt nothing. I went to the kitchen and washed dishes that were already clean. I dried them. I put them away. I wiped the counter. I wiped it again. My mom called. I let it go to voicemail. I listened to the voicemail. She wanted to know if I was coming for Sunday dinner. I called her back. I said yes. I made my voice sound the way it always sounded. I did not say what I knew. I would not say it for another six months.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Alex took the test and got the results and learned he had been adopted at birth. His parents had not told him. He was forty-one. He sat at his computer in the room he had once shared with his brother. He looked around. The walls were the same color they had been when he was twelve. He had inherited the house. From his parents. Who were not, biologically, his parents. He stood up. He went downstairs. He made coffee. He drank it on the back porch. The sun was rising. The birds were starting. He sat there until the coffee was cold. He went to work.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: She messaged me through the DNA site. "Hi, I think we share a father." I read it on the train. The train was crowded. I looked up at the people. They were on their phones too. I looked back down. I read it again. I did not respond for three weeks. When I finally did, I wrote "Hi." That was it. She wrote back the same day. We exchanged a few sentences. I closed the app. I did not open it again for a month. The information was in my pocket. I carried it like a coin. Sometimes I felt it. Sometimes I forgot.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Pilar got the email at her sister's birthday party. The email was from a man who said he was her half-brother. She read the email in her sister's bathroom. She read it twice. She came back out. She sang Happy Birthday. She helped cut the cake. She handed the slices around. She ate her own slice. She watched her sister open presents. She drove home. She did not tell her sister. She sat at her own kitchen table. The cake had been good. She thought about that. She thought about the email. She did not respond. She would. She turned off the light.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: My father had another child. He never told us. He died eight years ago. The half-sister found me on Facebook. She was kind in her message. She included a photo. She had his eyes. I sat at my desk and looked at the photo for a long time. I went and got my photo album. I found a picture of my dad at my high school graduation. I held them up. I felt nothing dramatic. I just felt thick, like wading. I would write back. I would. I made dinner. I watched the news. I went to bed. The photo was still up on my screen when I closed the laptop.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Tobias learned about the half-sister in his mother's will, after she died. The bequest specified an amount to a name he did not know. The lawyer said he could explain. Tobias did not ask him to explain that day. He went home. He did the laundry. He took out the trash. He fed the cat. He sat at the kitchen table and looked at his mother's handwriting on a recipe card. He had so much to do. The estate. The house. Now this. He would call the lawyer Monday. He turned out the light. He went to bed. He slept poorly. He got up. He went to work.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: I learned about my half-brother from my aunt at my mother's wake. She told me at the buffet table. I had a plate of ham. I held the plate. She kept talking. She said it had been a thing in the family for thirty years. I nodded. I said, "Okay." I went and sat down. I ate the ham. I ate the cheese. I did not eat the cookie. I slid the cookie onto my husband's plate. He gave me a look. I shook my head. He didn't ask again. We drove home in silence. I would tell him about my brother. After we got home. After I slept.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Bryan saw the headlines on Twitter. The author whose books had gotten him through his divorce, his mother's death, his son's autism diagnosis, had lifted entire passages from other writers. The receipts were extensive. Bryan scrolled them. He closed Twitter. He went to his bookshelf. He looked at the row of her novels, twelve of them, the spines worn. He did not know what to do. He sat on the rug. He pulled one out. He flipped through it. The lines he had loved were the lines that had been stolen. He put the book back. He went and made dinner. He left the books where they were.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: I read the expose on my phone in the line at CVS. By the end I had moved up two spots. The cashier was a kid who did not look at me. I paid for my toothpaste. I walked to my car. I sat in the parking lot. I had been recommending her books to friends for fifteen years. I had given them as gifts. I had taught one of her short stories to my freshman comp class. I drove home. I went to my office. I looked at the syllabus. I would not teach her again. I would. I would change the syllabus. I would do it next semester. I would.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Vanessa heard the news on a podcast while folding laundry. She kept folding. She matched socks. She paired them. She put them in piles. The hosts went on. Vanessa did not stop. She finished the laundry. She put it away. She came back to the living room. She sat on the couch. The author had been her hero in college. She had written her senior thesis on her work. She thought about throwing the books away. She did not. She sat for a while longer. She got up. She made dinner. She did not look at the books. She did not look away from them either.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: My book club met to discuss her latest. Halfway through, someone showed us the article on her phone. We all read it. We were quiet for a long time. Then we were less quiet. Then we were quiet again. I poured myself another glass of wine. I drank it slowly. I had been the one to pick the book. I felt sheepish. Mostly I felt the way I felt when something I had counted on broke. Not loudly. Just a small giving-way. We did not finish the discussion. We moved on to the gossip. I drove home. I did not pick a book for next month.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Henry had read every novel of hers, twice. The expose came out on a Tuesday. He read the side-by-side comparisons. They were undeniable. He went outside and sat on his stoop. The street was quiet. A neighbor walked past with a dog. The dog stopped to sniff Henry's shoe. The neighbor apologized. Henry waved it off. The neighbor moved on. Henry stayed on the stoop. The sun went down. The streetlights came on. He thought about the books on his shelf. He went inside. He turned out the lights. He went to bed without dinner. He woke up hungry at three. He drank water. He went back to sleep.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: The gate agent announced another two hours at 11:47 PM. I had been at the airport since two. The wedding had started at six. I was the maid of honor. I sat in the plastic chair and looked at my phone. Forty-three messages from the bridal party. I read them all. I did not respond. I would respond when I landed. I bought a sandwich. I ate the sandwich. The bread was stale. I sat with my hand on my carry-on. I closed my eyes. I was not crying. I was past crying. I just wanted to be somewhere with a bed and a closed door.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Marisol watched her connection peel away from the gate without her. She had been running. She had not made it. She stood at the empty jet bridge. She was sweating in her travel clothes. The agent at the next desk said the next flight was tomorrow morning. Marisol nodded. She had been planning to give the eulogy at her grandmother's funeral. The funeral was that afternoon. She walked to a gate-side chair. She sat down. She did not call her family. She typed a text and saved it as a draft. She put her phone in her pocket. She closed her eyes. She did not sleep.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: I missed my daughter's recital because of the storm in Dallas. I sat at the gate and watched the snow on the screen. I called my wife. She held up the phone for me. I heard the music. I heard her play her piece. I cried, but not loudly, because I was at gate B14 and people were eating Cinnabon. The clapping came through the phone. I clapped too, quietly. I told my daughter she was wonderful. She said, "You weren't there." I said I knew. I told her I was sorry. She said it was okay. We hung up. I sat for a long time.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Tom was at the gate when the announcement came. Cancelled. He had a job interview in Chicago in nineteen hours. He had been planning to take the red-eye. The red-eye was now nothing. He stood up. He walked to the customer service line. The line was forty people long. He took his place. He did not look at his phone. He did not check his email. He waited. He moved up. He moved up. He moved up. By the time he reached the agent, he had decided not to bother. He turned around. He walked to baggage claim. He took the train home.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: I sat at the gate as the delay grew, hour by hour. My brother was getting married at four. It was now eight, two thousand miles away. The ceremony was over. The reception was probably ending. I had a tuxedo in my carry-on, with the tie I had practiced for a week. I did not change clothes. I did not eat. I just sat. The gate agent finally said we were boarding. I boarded. I sat in 14C. I looked out the window. The plane took off. I did not feel relief. I just closed my eyes. The wedding was over. The plane flew.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Sandra found the dog in her tomato bed for the third time that week. He was a good dog. He looked at her. She looked at him. She put down her coffee. She walked him back to the neighbor's gate. She knocked. The neighbor answered. The neighbor said, "Oh, sorry," the same way she had said it Monday and Tuesday. Sandra said it was fine. It was not fine. She walked back to her house. She picked up her coffee. The coffee was cold. She did not drink it. She went inside. She did not bother to fix the tomatoes. She would do it tomorrow. Or not.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: The dog was on my porch again. He wagged at me through the screen. I sighed. I opened the door. He came in. He went to the dog bed I had bought specifically for these visits. He lay down. I texted my neighbor: he's here. She wrote back: be over in ten. The dog slept. I made tea. I sat with him. I did not feel angry. I did not feel anything in particular. I just felt like I had been doing this for so long that it had become a kind of routine. The neighbor came. The dog left. I washed the tea cup.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Reggie was woken by barking at five AM. The neighbor's dog. Again. He lay in bed for a while. He hoped the dog would leave on his own. The dog did not. Reggie got up. He pulled on jeans. He went outside in his slippers. The dog was on his lawn, doing his business. Reggie waited. The dog finished. Reggie walked the dog back. He left the dog at the neighbor's gate. He came home. He climbed back into bed. His wife asked. He said, "Same." She patted his shoulder. He did not fall back asleep. He got up at six and made coffee.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: I had stopped putting the chairs back upright. The dog kept knocking them over. There was no point. I just left them on their sides. My husband asked. I said, "It's the dog." He said, "What dog." I said, "You know." He went out and stood the chairs back up. By the next afternoon they were over again. He stopped standing them up too. We had a yard full of fallen chairs. I called the neighbor once. She apologized. The chairs kept falling. I did not call again. The chairs kept falling.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Maeve found the dog in her shed for the fifth time. She had stopped being startled. She squatted down. She scratched his head. He licked her hand. She got him on a leash she now kept in the shed. She walked him home. The neighbor opened the door. "Again," the neighbor said. Maeve said, "Yeah." The neighbor said she'd reinforced the fence. Maeve said okay. They had had this exact conversation before. They both knew. Maeve walked back across the lawn. The leash dragged behind her. The dog was inside. She put the leash back in the shed.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I sent the message to Gary instead of Gabby. The message said, "Gary is the worst." I saw the green bubble. I saw his name. I felt my whole body slow down. I did not delete it because deleting it would not delete it from his end. I just looked at it. He started typing. I watched the dots. I waited. I felt very calm in a way that was not calm. He sent: "Yikes." I wrote back, "I am so sorry." He didn't respond. I closed the phone. I left it face down on the counter. I made dinner. I would deal with him later.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Felicia sent the photo to her boss instead of her best friend. The photo was of her boss. She had been complaining about him. She saw the message go through. She did not move. The little check turned blue. He had read it. She set the phone down. She got up. She walked to the kitchen. She poured a glass of water. She drank it. She sat at the kitchen table. She did not check her phone. She did not respond. She would. Eventually. She put her head down on the table. The wood was cool. She closed her eyes.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I texted my sister-in-law something I should have only texted my sister. About my mother-in-law. About the dinner. The thread was clearly wrong; it had Andrea's name at the top. I had been on five hours of sleep. I had been on five hours of sleep for two months. I closed the phone. I did not even try to recall the message. I just closed the phone. I went to the kitchen. I made tea. I drank it. I sat in the rocking chair with my eyes closed. I would write Andrea an apology. Tomorrow. Maybe the day after. Maybe I would just let it sit.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Aaron sent the venting message to the group chat instead of to his wife. The group chat included the people he was venting about. He saw it the second after he sent it. He stared. He did not type. He did not delete. He let the messages start coming in. They came in. He read them. He closed the chat. He went outside. He sat on the porch. He looked at the street. The street was empty. He thought about apologizing. He thought about explaining. He could not find the energy for either. He went back inside. He went to bed at eight thirty. He turned off his phone.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I texted my doctor a meme meant for my husband. The meme was inappropriate. The doctor was my new GP. We had not yet met in person. I read the screen for a long time. I did not type anything. I made coffee. I sat in the chair by the window. The sun was bright. I held the cup. I looked at my phone. I would just have to mention it at my appointment next month. Maybe she wouldn't remember. Maybe she would. I drank the coffee. I refilled the cup. I sat. The phone did not buzz back. I closed my eyes for a while.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Mei read the email from the president sitting cross-legged on her dorm room floor. The college was closing in May. She was a junior. She read the email. She closed her laptop. She got up. She went to the window. The quad was full of people not yet knowing. She watched them for a while. She sat back down on the floor. She did not call her parents. She did not call her advisor. She lay back. She looked at the ceiling. She had moved into this room three weeks ago. She thought about the boxes she had not yet unpacked. She did not unpack them.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: I had been at this college for fifteen years as faculty. The president sent the email at four PM on a Friday. I read it in my office, alone. I had a stack of papers to grade. I graded them. I closed my laptop. I locked my office. I walked to my car. I drove home. I did not turn on the radio. I sat in my driveway for twenty minutes. The garage door was closed. I did not open it. My wife came out. She knocked on the window. I rolled it down. She said, "Are you okay?" I said, "They're closing the school." She said, "Oh."

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Diego heard about the closure from a campus tour group walking past. The guide was using the past tense. Diego, walking the other way to class, slowed. He kept walking. He went to his class. He sat down. He listened to the lecture. He did not take notes. He did not take notes for the rest of the day. He went home. He sat at his kitchen table. He had transferred here from another college that had also closed. He thought about that. He laughed once. It was not really a laugh. He went to bed at seven. He did not eat. He slept a long time.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: I was the dean of admissions. I had to start writing the email to the incoming class telling them not to come. I had been recruiting them for a year. I knew their names. I sat at my desk. I wrote the first sentence. I deleted it. I wrote it again. I deleted it. I got up. I made coffee. I came back. I wrote the sentence. I left it. I wrote the next sentence. I left that too. I sent the draft to my supervisor at midnight. I got home at one. I sat in the kitchen. I did not turn on a light. I went to bed.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Aisha learned the news in her sociology class. The professor announced it. He had tears in his eyes. Some students cried. Some students looked at their phones. Aisha did neither. She sat in her seat. She put her pen down. She looked at the whiteboard. The whiteboard had a diagram about social mobility. The diagram was not finished. The professor did not finish it. The class ended early. Aisha walked to the bookstore. She bought a hoodie with the school's name on it. She went home. She put it in a drawer. She did not wear it. She would. Maybe.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: The nurse called me to clarify a result. As we talked, it became clear that the result wasn't mine. It belonged to another woman with my last name. I sat at the kitchen table while she explained. I had been preparing, for two weeks, to receive a serious diagnosis. I had cried. I had told my sister. I had told my husband. I had not told my children. Now there was no diagnosis. There was somebody else's diagnosis. I thanked the nurse. I hung up. I sat. I did not call my sister. I did not call my husband. I just sat. I would call. Tomorrow. I made tea.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Roberto discovered the mix-up when his portal showed test results for someone else's pregnancy. He was a sixty-eight-year-old man. He laughed once. Then he stopped laughing. He called the office. They put him on hold. He waited eighteen minutes. He hung up. He called back. He waited again. The woman who answered was apologetic. She would fix it. She would. He thanked her. He hung up. He sat in his recliner. The TV was on mute. He looked at it. The news was about something he didn't understand. He did not turn up the volume. He did not turn it off. He just sat.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I called for my own results and they read me someone else's. I caught it because the patient had a different birth year. The receptionist apologized. She put me on hold. She came back. She apologized again. She said it would take a few days to sort out. I said okay. I hung up. I sat in the parking lot of the grocery store. I had been about to go in. I did not go in. I drove home. I sat on my couch. The fridge was empty. I would have to go grocery shopping. I would go tomorrow. I ordered a pizza. I waited for it. I ate two slices.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Kalinda's chart had three other people's allergies on it. She noticed during a pre-op consultation. She told the surgeon. The surgeon paused. The surgeon called the records office. The records office called the records office at the other hospital. There was a lot of calling. Kalinda sat on the exam table with the paper crinkling under her. The surgery was rescheduled. She drove home. She would have to take more time off work. She would have to call her boss. She did not call. She made dinner. She watched a show. She fell asleep on the couch with her shoes on. She woke at three. She went to bed.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I got a bill for a procedure I never had. I called billing. They said it was correct. I said it wasn't. They said they would look into it. They did not look into it. I called again. They said someone else with my name and date of birth had had the procedure. They said they would correct it. They had been saying they would correct it for two months. The bill kept coming. The bill kept being sent to collections. I sat with the latest envelope unopened on my counter for three days. I would call again. I would. I made my coffee. I went to work.
